---
title: "Integrals"
engine: julia
---

```{julia}
#| echo: false
using ConvolutionInterpolations, CairoMakie, Printf
```

A negative `derivative` order gives an interpolant of an integral: `derivative = -1` is the
antiderivative, `-2` the twofold integral, and so on. Like the derivatives, integrals are
evaluated analytically from the kernel's polynomial pieces, not by quadrature, and they are
anchored at the first knot: there the integral is zero, and so are all lower integrals. So the
antiderivative evaluated at $b$ is $\int_{x_0}^{b}$ of the interpolant, and a definite integral
between two limits is the difference of two evaluations.

## A first example

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Julia

```{julia}
x = range(0, 2π, length = 40)                             # 40 uniformly spaced samples
y = sin.(x)                                               # the values at the samples
i1 = convolution_interpolation(x, y; derivative = -1)     # the integral from x[1] = 0
i2 = convolution_interpolation(x, y; derivative = -2)     # the twofold integral, also anchored at 0

a, b = 1.0, 2.5                                           # the limits of a definite integral
i1(1.0), i2(1.0), i1(b) - i1(a)                           # 1 − cos(1), 1 − sin(1), cos(a) − cos(b)
```

## Python

```python
import numpy as np
from convinterp import convolution_interpolation

x = np.linspace(0.0, 2 * np.pi, 40)                       # 40 uniformly spaced samples
y = np.sin(x)                                             # the values at the samples
i1 = convolution_interpolation(x, y, derivative=-1)       # the integral from x[0] = 0
i2 = convolution_interpolation(x, y, derivative=-2)       # the twofold integral, also anchored at 0

a, b = 1.0, 2.5                                           # the limits of a definite integral
i1(1.0), i2(1.0), i1(b) - i1(a)                           # 1 − cos(1), 1 − sin(1), cos(a) − cos(b)
```

:::

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
println("| | ∫₀¹ f | ∫₀¹∫₀ˢ f | ∫ₐᵇ f |")
println("|:--|--:|--:|--:|")
@printf("| interpolant | %.12f | %.12f | %.12f |\n", i1(1.0), i2(1.0), i1(b) - i1(a))
@printf("| exact | %.12f | %.12f | %.12f |\n", 1 - cos(1.0), 1 - sin(1.0), cos(a) - cos(b))
```

## Integrals don't cost convergence order

Where each derivative order costs one order of convergence, integrals cost none: the integral
of the interpolant converges at least as fast as the interpolant itself. Runge's function with
`:b7`, the interpolant and its first and second integrals:

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "The convergence study"
runge(x) = 1 / (1 + 25x^2)                                # Runge's function
irunge = (x -> (atan(5x) + atan(5)) / 5,                  # its integral from −1
          x -> (x * (atan(5x) + atan(5)) - log(1 + 25x^2) / 10 + log(26) / 10) / 5)  # its twofold integral from −1
xr = range(-1, 1, length = 2001)                          # fine points for measuring the error
ns = [41, 81, 161, 321, 641, 1281]                        # the numbers of samples
hs = 2 ./ (ns .- 1)                                       # the corresponding spacings
orders = 0:-1:-2                                          # the interpolant and two integrals
exact = (runge, irunge...)                                # the function and its integrals

errors = [begin
              xn = range(-1, 1, length = n)
              itp_m = convolution_interpolation(xn, runge.(xn); kernel = :b7, derivative = m)
              maximum(abs.(itp_m.(xr) .- exact[1-m].(xr)))
          end for n in ns, m in orders]

fig = Figure(size = (800, 420))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xscale = log10, yscale = log10, xreversed = true,
          xlabel = "spacing h", ylabel = "largest error")
for (j, m) in enumerate(orders)
    scatterlines!(ax, hs, max.(errors[:, j], 1e-17); markersize = 8,
                  label = m == 0 ? "interpolant" : "integral order $(-m)")
end
Legend(fig[1, 2], ax)
fig
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
observed = [begin
                e = errors[:, j]
                i = findlast(v -> v > 1e-13, e); i = max(i, 2)   # the finest grid still clear of rounding
                log(e[i-1] / e[i]) / log(hs[i-1] / hs[i])
            end for j in eachindex(orders)]
println("| | interpolant | integral order 1 | integral order 2 |")
println("|:--|--:|--:|--:|")
println("| observed convergence order | ", join((@sprintf("%.2f", o) for o in observed), " | "), " |")
```

Evaluating an integral costs about the same as evaluating the interpolant, whatever the number
of knots: the contribution of every knot left of the stencil is a polynomial in the position
within the cell, and those are precomputed when the interpolant is built. Each kernel supports
integrals up to a fixed order, 2 for `:a0` and `:a1`, 4 for the other `:a` kernels, 6 for
`:b5` and 8 for `:b7` to `:b13`; the precomputed tables grow with the order, so high orders in
several dimensions cost memory.

## Integrals in more dimensions

In more dimensions the orders are given per axis, and integrals combine freely with
interpolation and derivatives along the other axes. The antiderivative along every axis is the
iterated integral from the corner of the grid; a derivative along one axis and an integral
along another is a Leibniz-rule operator, in one evaluation:

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Julia

```{julia}
xg = range(0, 2π, length = 60)                            # knots along x
yg = range(0, 2π, length = 60)                            # knots along y
data = [sin(xi) * cos(yi) for xi in xg, yi in yg]         # sin(x)·cos(y) on the grid

ixy = convolution_interpolation((xg, yg), data; derivative = (-1, -1))   # ∫∫ from (0, 0)
ix  = convolution_interpolation((xg, yg), data; derivative = (-1, 0))    # ∫ dx, interpolated in y
dxiy = convolution_interpolation((xg, yg), data; derivative = (1, -1))   # ∂/∂x ∫ dy

ixy(1.0, 2.0), ix(1.0, 2.0), dxiy(1.0, 2.0)
```

## Python

```python
xg = np.linspace(0.0, 2 * np.pi, 60)                      # knots along x
yg = np.linspace(0.0, 2 * np.pi, 60)                      # knots along y
data = np.sin(xg)[:, None] * np.cos(yg)[None, :]          # sin(x)·cos(y) on the grid

ixy = convolution_interpolation((xg, yg), data, derivative=(-1, -1))    # ∫∫ from (0, 0)
ix  = convolution_interpolation((xg, yg), data, derivative=(-1, 0))     # ∫ dx, interpolated in y
dxiy = convolution_interpolation((xg, yg), data, derivative=(1, -1))    # ∂/∂x ∫ dy

ixy(1.0, 2.0), ix(1.0, 2.0), dxiy(1.0, 2.0)
```

:::

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
println("| at (1, 2) | ∫₀¹∫₀² f | ∫₀¹ f dx | ∂/∂x ∫₀² f dy |")
println("|:--|--:|--:|--:|")
@printf("| interpolant | %.12f | %.12f | %.12f |\n", ixy(1.0, 2.0), ix(1.0, 2.0), dxiy(1.0, 2.0))
@printf("| exact | %.12f | %.12f | %.12f |\n", (1 - cos(1.0)) * sin(2.0), (1 - cos(1.0)) * cos(2.0), cos(1.0) * sin(2.0))
```

## Discontinuous data

The `:a0` kernel, which is nearest-neighbour interpolation, integrates piecewise-constant data
exactly: a spike one cell wide and $1/h$ high integrates to a unit step, which is how a
sampled impulse should behave.

```{julia}
n = 1001                                                  # knots
xs = range(0, 2π, length = n)
h = step(xs)                                              # the spacing
spike = [abs(xi - π) < h / 2 ? 1 / h : 0.0 for xi in xs]  # a unit-area spike at π
F = convolution_interpolation(xs, spike; kernel = :a0, derivative = -1)   # its integral

xf = range(0, 2π, length = 801)
fig = Figure(size = (800, 400))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "x")
lines!(ax, xf, F.(xf); label = "∫ spike")
lines!(ax, xf, (xf .> π) .* 1.0; color = :black, linestyle = :dash, label = "unit step")
Legend(fig[1, 2], ax)
fig
```

## Nonuniform grids

Integrals are available on uniform grids only, in both packages; the nonuniform kernels of the
Julia package support interpolation and derivatives but not antiderivatives. The
[nonuniform page](nonuniform.qmd) says what to do instead.
